rows.answer:
Keep the supplied code unchanged: `sum_valid<<<1, 96, 0, stream>>>(device_input, device_output, valid);` runs one block of 96 threads for every `valid` from 0 through 96, including zero.

In the original kernel at `valid=70`, threads 70–95 evaluate `threadIdx.x < valid` as false, skip the entire conditional—including the input load, shared-memory store, barrier, and summation—and reach the end of the kernel. Threads 0–69 enter the conditional and encounter `__syncthreads()` under a condition that is not uniform across the block. That violates the block-barrier contract and produces undefined behavior; it does not imply that every device must hang.

A successful `cudaGetLastError()` checks immediate launch errors, not completion or algorithmic correctness. Execution is asynchronous, so the host endpoint can remain responsive while the stream has unfinished work. A completion event that is not ready establishes only that it has not completed; the divergent-barrier report identifies the synchronization violation.

In the replacement, every shared-memory read by thread zero has an index `i` satisfying `0 <= i < valid <= 96`. Thread `i` exists, loads `input[i]`, and initializes `values[i]` before reaching the unconditional barrier. All 96 threads execute that barrier, which makes those writes visible before thread zero reads them; uninitialized entries at indices greater than or equal to `valid` are never read.

At `valid=0`, all 96 threads skip the loads but still execute the barrier. Thread zero initializes its local sum to `0.0f`, performs zero loop iterations, and writes `0.0f` to the device output. The kernel is neither skipped nor replaced by host-side output initialization.
